content: Ductal carcinoma is the most common type of breast cancer in women. It can be classified into two groups according to the Armed Forces Institute of Pathology (AFIP): large cell carcinoma in situ and small cell carcinoma in situ. The pathogenesis of ductal carcinoma is characterized by the microinvasion of cancer cells confined to the ducts, without extension beyond the basement membrane. Mutations in the HER2/neu gene have been associated with the development of ductal carcinoma. Ductal carcinoma was first described in 1893. It is classified into two main groups based on AFIP criteria: 1. Large cell carcinoma: This is a more aggressive form, also referred to as comedocarcinoma. 2. Small cell carcinoma: This is less aggressive and includes subtypes such as cribriform, micropapillary, papillary, and solid in situ. Other variants of ductal carcinoma include non-DCIS (ductal carcinoma in situ) entities. The pathophysiology of ductal carcinoma involves the microinvasion of cancer cells limited to the ducts, with no extension beyond the basement membrane. HER2/neu mutations are implicated in its development. Gross pathology findings typically include a white, firm stellate lesion. Microscopic histopathological analysis reveals characteristic findings such as evenly spaced cells with a cookie-cutter appearance and cells lining up along the lumen or glandular spaces, forming structures known as Roman bridges. Ductal carcinoma is most commonly observed in females aged 40 to 80 years and is rarely seen in males, typically between 60 and 70 years of age. It is more prevalent among postmenopausal women. There is no racial predilection for ductal carcinoma, and females are significantly more affected than males. Risk factors for ductal carcinoma include: A family history of breast cancer Mutations in BRCA1 or BRCA2 genes Previous exposure to radiation therapy Increased breast density Hormonal therapy Nulliparity (never having given birth) Obesity Most patients with ductal carcinoma remain asymptomatic for years. Early clinical features may include skin color changes or nipple discharge. If untreated, the disease may progress to lymph node invasion and metastasis. The most common complication is lymphedema. Prognosis depends on the histological subtype, with worse outcomes associated with younger age at diagnosis, Black ethnicity, and high-grade cancer. The diagnosis of ductal carcinoma is often made when specific diagnostic criteria are met. Symptoms may include nipple discharge, skin color changes, skin thickening with a warm sensation, an orange-peel appearance of the skin, or nipple retraction. Physical examination findings are often nonspecific, but in some cases, a palpable mass may be present. Laboratory findings may include positive or negative estrogen receptor (ER) and progesterone receptor (PR) expression. Mammography is the imaging modality of choice, with findings such as calcifications (most common), simple masses, soft-tissue opacities, or asymmetry without calcifications. Other diagnostic studies may also be used. Treatment for ductal carcinoma includes medical therapy and surgery. Medical therapy is divided into hormonal therapy and targeted therapy. Hormonal therapy involves selective estrogen receptor modulators like tamoxifen or raloxifene. Targeted therapy includes HER2-directed treatments such as trastuzumab. The primary goal of medical therapy is to reduce the risk of ipsilateral or contralateral breast invasion and recurrence. Response to therapy is monitored periodically. Surgery is the mainstay of treatment and includes options such as mastectomy or breast-conserving therapy, often combined with other treatments. Surgical approaches are tailored to individual patients. Prevention strategies for ductal carcinoma include secondary prevention measures such as screening mammography for women aged 50 to 74 years (or earlier if risk factors are identified) and regular breast self-examinations (BSE). Once diagnosed and successfully treated, patients are followed up every 3, 6, or 12 months, depending on individual assessments.
